awd_titl_txt: Conference: Pilot Peer Mentoring Program for Principle Investigators in the Scholarships in STEM Program
awd_abstract_narration:
This conference proposal will contribute to the national need for well-educated scientists, mathematicians, engineers, and technicians by supporting the principal investigators within the Scholarships in Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics (S-STEM) Program from institutions all over the country. The management of these large programs can be challenging and time intensive, and the hurdles in terms of recruitment and retention/graduation of high-achieving, low-income students with demonstrated financial need differs between institutional type and region. The goal of this program is to mentor up to 48 principal investigators (PIs) who are in their 1st or 2nd year of their S-STEM Grant. The mentees will be split up based on institutional type (e.g., private, state, research-heavy, 4-year primarily undergraduate or community college) and region (urban, suburban, rural, EPSCOR, ect.). This will allow the project to achieve two outcomes: First, a wide variety of PIs will be assisted, leading to more successful S-STEM programs in their early years of implementation. Second, surveys will be conducted and focus group data collected to generate broad and widely applicable recommendations for the effective and successful implementation of S-STEM programs.

The S-STEM program offers a wealth of knowledge focused on promoting student success. A mentoring program designed for S-STEM principal investigators (PIs) can similarly yield insights by identifying common institutional barriers and recruitment challenges, enabling the testing and tracking of effective solutions. The findings from this initiative could serve as a valuable resource for all S-STEM PIs and assist institutions in developing strategies to enhance the persistence of low-income students in STEM fields. Additionally, this program will provide direct support to newer PIs by minimizing the time spent navigating institutional obstacles, improving the effectiveness and efficiency of recruitment efforts, and helping the PIs articulate their successes and challenges to the NSF in their annual reports. Comparative surveys will be conducted between mentored PIs and those in their second or third year who did not receive mentoring to evaluate the perceived challenges of managing and implementing an S-STEM project, both with and without peer PI mentoring. This project is funded by NSF's Scholarships in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics program, which seeks to increase the number of academically talented low-income students with demonstrated financial need who earn degrees in STEM fields. It also aims to improve the education of future STEM workers, and to generate knowledge about academic success, retention, transfer, graduation, and academic/career pathways of low-income students.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The S-STEM Pilot Peer Mentoring Program was developed to address the challenges faced by many new principal investigators (PIs) running NSF Scholarships in STEM (S-STEM) programs. While S-STEM programs provide extensive mentoring and support for students, there has historically been no formal mentoring structure for the faculty responsible for implementing and managing these complex scholarship programs. New PIs are expected to navigate student recruitment, scholarship administration, financial aid processes, program evaluation, and student support while simultaneously managing their teaching, research, and service responsibilities.

This project developed and evaluated a national peer mentoring model that connected experienced S-STEM PIs with faculty who were new to the program. Fifty-three mentors and mentees representing institutions from 22 states participated in seven small mentoring groups that met monthly to discuss recruitment strategies, scholarship administration, student engagement, cohort building, program evaluation, and other challenges associated with implementing successful S-STEM programs. The mentoring groups created a community of practice where participants openly shared experiences, practical solutions, and effective strategies that could be adapted across a wide range of institution types.

An independent evaluation conducted by MN Associates found strong participant engagement and identified several recurring themes across the mentoring groups. Participants reported that recruitment of qualified scholars, scholarship distribution, institutional coordination, student engagement, and leadership development were common challenges regardless of institution type. The mentoring program provided a supportive environment in which principal investigators exchanged practical solutions, reduced professional isolation, and developed strategies that can improve the effectiveness and sustainability of S-STEM programs nationwide.

The project also produced resources that extend beyond the pilot itself. A comprehensive supplemental report documented the implementation of the mentoring program and synthesized lessons learned from ~35 mentoring meetings, while the independent evaluation documented participant feedback and recommendations for future implementation. Findings from the project were presented to the broader S-STEM community at the 2025 S-STEM Scholars Meeting hosted by the American Association for the Advancement of Science Resource and Evaluation Center (AAAS REC) and the AAAS-led New PI Bootcamp, where the findings were used to inform current and new PIs, and to recruit participants for subsequent mentoring cohorts.

The project's intellectual merit lies in developing and evaluating a scalable peer mentoring model that identified effective practices for supporting new S-STEM principal investigators. Its broader impacts include strengthening faculty leadership, improving implementation of S-STEM scholarship programs, disseminating best practices nationally through reports and presentations, and establishing a sustainable mentoring network that continues to benefit institutions and future STEM scholars across the United States.

The success of this pilot demonstrated strong demand for continued peer mentoring among S-STEM PIs. The model directly led to the development of a second, expanded mentoring program involving approximately 30 mentors and 60 mentees organized into 15 mentoring groups representing institutions from 34 U.S. states. While this second cohort is supported through a separate project, its successful expansion demonstrates the scalability and broader impact of the pilot mentoring model developed through this award.
